title: Dedicated IP vs Shared IP for Cold Email: What Actually Changes
metaTitle: Dedicated IP vs Shared IP for Cold Email (2026)
metaDescription: What genuinely differs between dedicated and shared IPs for cold email — who's steering your reputation, when each setup makes sense, and how to tell which one you're already on.
excerpt: On a dedicated IP, your sending reputation belongs to you alone. On a shared pool, it's an average of whoever else is sending from it. Here's when that distinction actually matters.

toc.title: What a shared IP pool is
Finding out what you're already on

contentHtml:
The short version: on a dedicated IP, your sending reputation is shaped by nothing but your own behavior. On a shared IP pool, your reputation is averaged across everyone else sending from that same pool, and you have zero say over who those other senders are. If your volume is low and your sending careful, a shared pool usually holds up fine. Once cold email is running at real scale, that lack of control becomes the whole problem.

I've personally seen a perfectly clean campaign land in spam because some stranger sharing the same pool got flagged that same morning. That's really the entire argument in one sentence. What follows is how each model actually functions, when each one is the right call, and how to figure out which one you're currently running on.

What a shared IP pool is

Most cold email platforms funnel your mail through a pool of IP addresses shared among hundreds, sometimes thousands, of their customers. Hit send, and the platform assigns whichever IP is next in the pool. Your message goes out from an address that dozens of unrelated businesses are also sending from.

The pool approach exists because it's cheap to run. The provider maintains a block of IPs, balances load across them, and never has to provision anything specific to your account. Efficient for them — but for you, it means the IP's reputation is a shared asset you don't fully own.

Google, Microsoft, and the rest assign reputation partly at the IP level. When the pool as a whole sends clean mail, you inherit that established trust without doing any warmup of your own. When a few senders in that same pool are careless or aggressive, you inherit their baggage too.

What a dedicated IP is

A dedicated IP is an address that only you send from — nobody else routes any mail through it. Every signal a mailbox provider picks up from that address, positive or negative, traces back to your own sending, and only yours.

That's simultaneously the upside and the burden. Your bounce rate, your complaint rate, how consistently you send, the quality of your list — all of it lands on an address that belongs to you alone. No neighbor to point at, and no neighbor dragging you down either.

A dedicated IP does need warmup. A fresh address starts with no reputation at all, so blasting 5,000 emails on the first day is off the table. You build volume gradually while the address earns trust. Solid platforms automate that ramp, but it's a real process and it takes a couple of weeks minimum.

Where they actually diverge: whose behavior sets your inbox placement

Cut through the marketing language and the real distinction is about control. On a shared pool, your placement is partly at the mercy of people you've never met. On a dedicated IP, it's entirely a function of what you do.

That distinction matters most when something breaks. On a dedicated IP, a deliverability dip has a traceable cause — your list, your copy, your volume, your authentication. You can dig in and fix it. On a shared pool, a dip might be your doing, or it might be the pool's, and you often have no way to tell which. You're troubleshooting blind, missing half the information.

It matters for consistency too. A dedicated IP you send from steadily builds a predictable pattern that mailbox providers learn to trust over time. A shared pool's reputation shifts as the mix of senders using it changes from one week to the next.

When shared IPs work fine

Shared pools aren't worthless — there are genuine situations where they're the right call.

  • Low volume. Sending a few hundred emails a month to a warm-ish list means the pool's built-in reputation is doing you a favor, and a dedicated IP would just mean extra warmup with no real payoff.
  • You're brand new and still testing. Before you even know if cold email works for your offer, a shared pool lets you start sending today without a warmup ramp slowing you down.
  • The pool is actually well managed. Some providers police their pools aggressively, remove bad senders quickly, and keep the addresses clean. A tightly run pool can beat a poorly warmed dedicated IP.

The honest way to put it: shared pools trade away control in exchange for convenience. If you don't need the control yet, that trade is a reasonable one.

When dedicated becomes necessary

The case for going dedicated gets compelling fast once cold email is a real, load-bearing channel for you.

  • You're sending real volume. Once you're past roughly 10,000 to 20,000 emails a month, you're generating enough signal to build and hold your own reputation — and enough is riding on it to want control over it.
  • You're running client campaigns. Agencies can't let one client's aggressive sending burn deliverability for another client. Isolation between accounts isn't a nice extra here — it's the actual product.
  • Deliverability is the channel itself. If one bad week of placement costs you real pipeline, you cannot afford a reputation you don't control.
  • You've already been burned once. If you've watched clean campaigns quietly slide to spam with no obvious cause, that cause was very likely the pool.

The diagnosis headache nobody mentions

The most underrated downside of a shared pool isn't the averaged-out reputation — it's that you lose the ability to actually debug problems.

On a dedicated IP, a deliverability drop happens inside a closed system. Check your bounce rate, check spam complaints, check authentication, check where your recent list came from — the cause is somewhere in there, because nothing else touches that IP.

On a shared pool, the cause could sit entirely outside your own account. You can scrub your list, rewrite your copy, and rewarm your mailboxes, and still see no improvement, because the real problem was three other senders you'll never even know about. Days get burned chasing down a problem that was never yours to begin with.

Comparing the two, side by side

FactorShared IP poolDedicated IP
Reputation controlShared across every sender on the poolEntirely yours
Warmup neededNo, inherits pool reputationYes, gradual ramp over ~2 weeks
Neighbor riskHigh — a bad actor on the pool can drag you down with themNone to speak of
Diagnosing problemsDifficult, since the cause may sit outside your account entirelyStraightforward — a closed system that's fully yours
Best forLow-volume senders and early-stage testingReal volume, agencies, and anyone where deliverability is mission-critical
CostUsually bundled in, sometimes the cheaper optionOften locked behind higher-priced tiers elsewhere

Finding out what you're already on

Most cold email tools don't make this easy to figure out, which is itself worth noting. Three ways to check:

  • Read the pricing page closely. If dedicated IPs get a mention at all, they're usually locked behind a pricier tier. If IPs never come up, you're almost certainly on a shared pool.
  • Look at your email headers. Send yourself a test message, pull up the raw headers, and check the sending IP. Feed it into a blacklist checker and see how many unrelated domains resolve to that same address.
  • Just ask support. Ask directly whether your account sends from a dedicated IP or a shared pool. A clear answer tells you something. A vague one tells you something too.

Choosing a platform

If you're picking a new cold email platform or switching off an old one, treat the IP model as a question worth asking upfront, not an afterthought. Plenty of well-known tools run every account below their top-tier plan on shared pools. That's the default across most of the category, which is exactly why it's worth checking before you commit.

Sendbox took the opposite approach from the start. Every account gets dedicated IPs and isolated infrastructure from the entry plan onward, not reserved as an enterprise perk, because the whole premise is that your reputation should genuinely be yours. If you want to see how that stacks up against the shared-pool approach, the Sendbox vs Instantly and Sendbox vs Smartlead comparisons break it down directly, and the email infrastructure guide covers the providers underneath it all.

The decision itself isn't complicated. If you're still quietly testing whether cold email works for you, a shared pool is a fine place to start. The moment it becomes a channel you actually rely on, you want a reputation that no stranger can touch.

faqs.question: Is a dedicated IP always better than a shared IP?
faqs.answer: Not always. For low-volume sending or early testing, a well-run shared pool hands you an established reputation with no warmup required. A dedicated IP only pulls ahead once you're sending enough volume to build and sustain your own reputation — roughly north of 10,000 to 20,000 emails a month.

faqs.question: How much sending volume do I need before a dedicated IP is worth it?
faqs.answer: As a rough guideline, once you're consistently past 10,000 to 20,000 emails a month, you're generating enough signal to maintain your own IP reputation, and there's enough pipeline riding on it to justify wanting control. Below that threshold, the warmup overhead often isn't worth taking on.

faqs.question: Do I need to warm up a dedicated IP?
faqs.answer: Yes. A newly assigned dedicated IP starts with no reputation at all, so you build volume gradually over roughly two weeks while it earns trust with mailbox providers. Good platforms automate this ramp for you, but it's a real process — you can't shortcut it by sending full volume from day one.

faqs.question: Can one bad sender on a shared pool really hurt my deliverability?
faqs.answer: Yes. Mailbox providers assign reputation partly at the IP level, so if another sender on your pool triggers spam complaints or lands on a blacklist, mail from that same IP can get filtered harder — even while your own campaigns stay perfectly clean.

faqs.question: Does a dedicated IP guarantee inbox placement?
faqs.answer: No. A dedicated IP hands you control over your own reputation, but placement still depends on list quality, content, authentication, sending consistency, and how recipients engage. It removes the neighbor-risk problem — it doesn't remove the actual work.

faqs.question: Which cold email tools include dedicated IPs?
faqs.answer: Most popular tools reserve dedicated IPs for an enterprise tier, or skip offering them altogether, leaving standard accounts on shared pools by default. Sendbox includes dedicated IPs and isolated infrastructure on every plan, starting from the entry tier.
